item.content:encoded:
PIB Backgrounder
India Cine Hub
Streamlining Film-Shooting Permit Applications
Posted On: 22 SEP 2026 1:59PM by PIB Delhi

The India Cine Hub (ICH) is a single-window digital portal that simplifies film permits, visa processing, and vendor access for domestic and global creators. Managed by the National Film Development Corporation of India (NFDC), it eliminates multi-state bureaucratic friction by consolidating state approvals, police clearances, and co-production applications into one central system. This streamlined approach makes filming across India faster and far more accessible, helping fuel the country's rapidly growing entertainment economy.

Making Filmmaking Easy in India

India, renowned for its rich cultural art forms and vibrant films, is steadily emerging as a global powerhouse in film, television and online content creation. This sector alone generated USD 13.1 billion in revenue in the financial year 2024, up 18 percent since 2019. This growth is expected to continue at a rate of 6-10 percent in the coming years and is estimated to reach a combined revenue of about USD 17.5-19.7 billion in the financial year 2029. Fuelled by a young population, a rapidly expanding 5G network, and ultra-affordable data, India is rapidly expanding its content ecosystem.

India is not just producing films and digital content; it is also a thriving filming location for domestic and international filmmakers. Its diverse geography spans from the scenic Himalayas to the white-sand beaches in the Andaman & Nicobar Islands. Featuring UNESCO World Heritage sites like Rajasthan's forts and palaces, India has emerged as an attractive location for filmmakers and tourists alike.

The Government has been initiating a series of reforms to further incentivise filmmaking in India. One key measure the government has put in place is streamlining shooting permits for films and live events across Indian locations through the India Cine Hub (ICH).

The India Cine Hub (ICH) is a digital, single-window platform designed to streamline the process of obtaining film permits across the country. By simplifying regulatory procedures and facilitating coordination with relevant authorities, it promotes ease of doing business and strengthens India’s position as an attractive global filming destination. Through collaboration with States and Union Territories, the platform also enables them to showcase their diverse filming locations, infrastructure and resources, creating opportunities for tourism and local economic development. By bringing greater efficiency, transparency and accessibility to the filmmaking process, the India Cine Hub is creating a more enabling ecosystem for filmmakers and supporting India’s emergence as a preferred destination for film production.

Beyond film permits, the platform is expanding to support Live Event Permissions as the core digital infrastructure for the Live Events Development Cell (LEDC). Through a venue-mapping approach, event proposals are routed to relevant local authorities and nodal officers for centralized coordination-with 9 premier venues already onboarded.

India Cine Hub: Single Portal for Film Permits

Run by the National Film Development Corporation of India (NFDC), the ICH acts as a digital single-window portal for filming permits. The NFDC is mandated to promote Indian cinema. Furthermore, it operates as an organisation under the Indian Union Government.

NFDC: Promoting the Indian Film Industry

The NFDC was established in 1975 by the Government, and it is mandated with the promotion and growth of the Indian film industry. Over time, it expanded by absorbing the Film Finance Corporation, Indian Motion Picture Export Corporation, and, following a 2020 government mandate, the Films Division, Directorate of Film Festivals, National Film Archive of India, and Children’s Film Society, India. Today, it serves as a fully integrated entity for film development, production, promotion, and preservation across all Indian languages.

Main Focus:

1. Co-produces film projects through public-private partnerships.

2. Provides line production for foreign shoots in India and overseas animation services.

3. Hosts Film Bazaar India, a major South Asian co-production and distribution market alongside the International Film Festival of India (IFFI), Goa.

Core Principles

Mission: Foster cinematic excellence and cultural diversity by supporting multilingual Indian films.

Vision: Drive domestic and global appreciation for independent Indian cinema.

Objectives:

a.Nurture talent via script development, workshops, and co-productions.

b.Promote Indian culture through cinema worldwide.

c.Maintain an agile organisation responsive to industry needs.

Features of India Cine Hub

The India Cine Hub offers the following features to creators interested in filming content or hosting live events in India:

  1. Provides a unified portal for domestic and international creators to apply for filming permissions. It integrates state-level systems, providing a common application form for states without online processing.
  • International creators can apply for filming permissions through the ICH, which facilitates obtaining a Film Visa.
  1. Processes applications for permission to undertake co-production ventures and provides detailed guidelines regarding such treaties.

  1. Offers comprehensive guidelines on film visas, regulations, aerial filming, animal filming, forests, and filming at monuments.
  2. Provides a comprehensive GIS-based location directory and information on shooting locations, relevant permit authorities, and India's filming hubs.

India's Film Cities

India has various major production hubs, employing over 1.6 lakh people. The cities with such hubs are Mumbai, Hyderabad, Chennai, Kolkata, Bengaluru, Thiruvananthapuram/ Kochi, Guwahati, Bhubaneswar, and Delhi. Of these, three are established and pivotal film cities: Film City in Mumbai (Maharashtra), Ramoji Film City in Hyderabad (Telangana), and Noida Film City in Noida (Uttar Pradesh). These cities are contributing to India's emergence as a one-stop destination for media and entertainment services by attracting filmmakers from across the world.

Mumbai Film City

The Mumbai Film City in Goregaon, Mumbai, is one of the largest studio complexes in the world and has all the facilities that filmmakers need. It covers more than 520 acres and has approximately 42 outdoor shooting locations. Film City boasts a varied natural topography including hills, valleys and ravines, flat open spaces, natural woods, shrubbery and water bodies. The Film City was established in 1977 by the Maharashtra state government, and it was renamed Dadasaheb Phalke Chitranagari in the year 2001 to commemorate the founder of the Indian film Industry. 

Ramoji Film City (Hyderabad)

Ramoji Film City, set up by Ramoji Group in 1996, was certified by the Guinness World Records as the world’s largest film studio complex. It is also the world’s largest integrated film city and India's only thematic holiday destination. Nearly 40 Indian films can be produced simultaneously in the complex, manned by a workforce of 6,000 personnel. It is spread over 2,000 acres, provides over 500 locations, and can cater to 20 international films simultaneously.

Noida Film City

The Noida Film City has various film studios and media houses. It houses satellite channels, multiplex offices, publication companies, radio broadcasting, audio industry giants, and film companies. It is spread across 100 acres. It has 16 studios and 350 channels broadcasting to 162 countries. It is the hub of television and media businesses. Around 17,000 media professionals are engaged in Film City, generating a wider economic impact through employment and livelihood opportunities for approximately 1.5 lakh people across associated and supporting sectors.

Development of New Film Cities

Digital content and media are now one of the largest media segments in India. India is also one of the youngest (15-29 years) consumers of digital content, with a large cohort of content creators. This generation is not only driving demand for global content but also actively shaping trends through short-form video, gaming, live streaming, and vernacular content platforms. India's internet footprint is also expanding. Internet subscribers increased from 25.15 crore in 2014 to 109.2+ crore at the end of March 2026. Wireless data cost dropped drastically from Rs.308/GB in 2014 to Rs. 7.51/GB in 2026, making digital services more affordable. 5G services are now available in 99.9% of districts across all States and Union Territories.

With rising demand for digital content led by a digitally savvy consumer base, and expanding internet infrastructure coupled with affordable wireless data services, this sector is expected to explode. To keep up, states such as Uttar Pradesh, Punjab, Madhya Pradesh, Assam, Chhattisgarh, Odisha and Bihar are building film city infrastructure in collaboration with private players. Driven by regional cinema and filming incentives from states, employment in the segment may grow at ~3.2%, leading to employment of about 200,000 people across the country by 2030. India is rapidly transitioning from being the world’s largest consumer base for digital content to becoming a formidable global powerhouse in content creation, innovation, and distribution.

  1. Lists verified film and non-film resource directories detailing local vendors across states, including:
    1. Post-production companies
    2. Property rentals
    3. Filmmakers and talent
    4. Film studios
    5. Equipment rentals
    6. Casting agencies
    7. Catering units
    8. Hotels and accommodations
    9. Medical facilities
    10. Security services
    11. Travel operators

Promoting Indian Tourism Through Made in India Films

Indian films have often led to higher tourism. One of the many such films that promoted the Indian film industry is 3 Idiots. After the movie, tourist arrivals in Ladakh increased 2.4-fold, according to the EY-FICCI Report. Similarly, Krrish filmed in Singapore through a collaboration with the Singapore Tourism Board, boosted Indian tourists in the country from six to seven million. Beyond domestic hits and regional favorites like Rajasthan, India’s visual diversity and cost-effective production environment continue to attract major global projects, ranging from Oscar-winning films like Slumdog Millionaire and Life of Pi to original productions by global streaming platforms like Netflix and Amazon Prime.

Madhya Pradesh won the "Most Film Friendly State" award at the 68th National Film Awards for its inclusive tourism ecosystem, while states like Rajasthan, Uttar Pradesh, Keralam and Uttarakhand actively lure filmmakers with infrastructure incentives, government location fee waivers and subsidies of up to Rs. 2 crore. Film tourism generates local employment and pours into local rural economies, while showcasing and preserving India's cultural heritage.

  1. Built with robust encryption, the portal is scalable to handle large volumes of applications and user traffic.

Additionally, a dashboard tracks total applications, providing a breakdown of approvals across state, national, and international levels.

Positioning India as a Premier Filming Hub

India’s film industry, among the world’s largest, plays an important role in promoting film tourism by bringing lesser-known destinations into the public imagination and transforming filming locations into travel attractions that showcase the country’s diverse cultural heritage. Supporting this potential, the India Cine Hub (ICH) serves as a centralised, single-window platform that simplifies the regulatory processes associated with film production. Filmmakers can apply online for shooting permits, while applications are digitally routed to relevant Ministries and State Nodal Officers, facilitating coordination for multi-agency clearances, location permissions, and film visas through a streamlined process.

Swachhata Hi Seva 2026 Campaign: Ministry of Textiles and Its Organisations Undertake Cleanliness and Awareness Activities
Posted On: 22 SEP 2026 1:28PM by PIB Delhi

Ministry of Textiles proudly announces the commencement of the Swachhta Hi Seva- 2026 Campaign, a nationwide initiative aimed at reinforcing the commitment to cleanliness and hygiene in everyday life. The campaign is celebrated across all organisations under the Ministry of Textiles from 17th September to 2nd October-2026.

This year’s theme, ‘Swachhata Mein Sahbhag, Swachh Bharat Viksit Bharat’, emphasizes celebrating cleanliness as a collective effort and festival of community involvement.  Under this theme, the Ministry and its affiliated organizations will be conducting a series of initiatives focused on hygiene, environmental conservation, and civic awareness. Cleanliness drives will be carried out in office premises, campuses of educational institutions, public areas, encouraging active involvement from employees, students, civil society groups, local communities and public at large.

Ministry has carried out following activities with commencement of the campaign.

  • Ministry of Textiles has conducted a Thematic Art Poster Making Competition on 18.09.2026 at GPOA-3 Netaji Nagar, New Delhi. All Division heads of the Ministry also visited various sections to review cleanliness and encouraged employees to adopt hygienic practices under Swachhata Hi Seva-2026.

  • Banner of Swachhta Hi Seva has been uploaded on the dashboard of the websites of the Ministry and its all organizations.

  • Standees have been installed at prominent places in the office building in the Ministry and other organizations.
  • Selfie point have been installed at prominent places in the office building in the Ministry and other organizations.

Central Cottage Industries Corporation of India Ltd. organized a Swachhata awareness session on 17 September 2026 to all make citizen aware of importance of Swachhata in our life.

Posters / Wall Massages relating to Swachhata & Water Conservation displayed in various places within showroom on 18/09/2026.

THE COTTON CORPORATION OF INDIA LTD-

The initiative promoted cleanliness awareness, strengthened citizen participation, and enhanced the visibility of the SHS campaign.

item.content:encoded:
Ministry of Information & Broadcasting
National Film Awards to Reach the Country’s Best Tourist Destinations
Union Minister Ashwini Vaishnaw Invites States to Propose Their Best Tourism Destinations for the Next National Film Awards
 National Film Awards Will Move Beyond Conference Rooms and Reach the People: Ashwini Vaishnaw
Posted On: 22 SEP 2026 1:09PM by PIB Delhi

Union Minister for Information and Broadcasting, Shri Ashwini Vaishnaw, today said that the National Film Awards are being taken to the country’s best tourist destinations, inspired by the vision of Prime Minister Shri Narendra Modi to take national events beyond conventional venues and connect them with destinations across the country.

🎬 Taking the National Film Awards to India’s finest tourist destinations! 🇮🇳 ✨

◉ Guided by the vision of Prime Minister @narendramodi, we are taking the #NationalFilmAwards to some of the finest tourist destinations across the country.

◉ #EktaNagar is renowned across the… pic.twitter.com/3yqgGjquDd

— PIB India (@PIB_India) September 22, 2026

Interacting with the media, Shri Ashwini Vaishnaw said, “We are taking the National Film Awards to the best tourist destinations in the country, inspired by the Hon’ble Prime Minister Shri Narendra Modi ji.”

He said that Ekta Nagar has gained recognition across the world and is a highly attractive destination, home to the world’s tallest statue of Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel. He added that when the Hon’ble President of India and leading personalities from the Indian film industry from across the country visit such a renowned tourist destination, it would provide an opportunity for more people to learn about and experience the destination.

The Minister said that the endeavour is to take the National Film Awards beyond a conference room and bring them closer to the people, while promoting and advancing them through tourism.

Shri Ashwini Vaishnaw invited all States to submit proposals identifying their best tourism destinations for hosting the National Film Awards. He said that the proposals should include the best facilities as well as a plan for 360-degree development of the destination. The State whose proposal is selected will host the subsequent National Film Awards at the proposed tourist destination.

The Minister recalled that when Prime Minister Shri Narendra Modi hosted the G20, its events were taken to different parts of the country and held across various States. He said that the National Film Awards are also being taken across the country as part of a larger thought process to explore how film and tourism can be brought together.

Shri Ashwini Vaishnaw said that bringing film and tourism together would benefit the tourist destination as well as enable the National Film Awards to move beyond a conference room and reach real physical destinations across the country.

*****

Mahesh Kumar/ Aparajita Priyadarshini

item.content:encoded:
Ministry of Communications
TRAI releases Telecom Consumer Protection (Thirteenth Amendment) Regulations, 2026
Posted On: 22 SEP 2026 1:04PM by PIB Delhi

The Telecom Regulatory Authority of India (TRAI) today released the Telecom Consumer Protection (Thirteenth Amendment) Regulation, 2026.

TRAI had released the draft Telecom Consumer Protection (Thirteenth Amendment) Regulations (TCPR), 2026 for consultation on its website on 07.04.2026. Since the implementation of TCPR (Twelfth Amendment), 2024, the Authority observed the limitation in the availability of Voice-and-SMS-only Special Tariff Vouchers (STVs)  being offered by telecom service providers, where only a limited number of such STVs, concentrated on longer validities were being offered and making low-income consumers deprived of affordable shorter duration choices. In order to address this concern, the draft TCPR (Thirteenth Amendment) consultation was issued.

In response to the draft Amendment, a total of 1132 responses were received from stakeholders. An Open House Discussion (OHD) on the consultation paper was also held on 15.06.2026.

Based on the responses received from the stakeholders and on its own analysis, TRAI has finalised the Telecom Consumer Protection (Thirteenth Amendment) Regulation, 2026.

The salient feature of this amendment is to mandate STVs with appropriate reduction in tariff, exclusively for Voice and SMS for:

  1. validities corresponding to each validity period of thirty days and less than thirty days for STV being offered for Voice, SMS and data and;
  2. validity renewable on the same date of every month and if the date of such renewal is not available in a month, the date of renewal shall be the last date of that month and;
  3. at least one STV with validity more than (i) and (ii) above, corresponding to the validity period of STVs being offered for Voice, SMS and data.

The Authority is of the view that such a tariff framework would sufficiently address consumer requirements. This amended regulation will provide low-income consumers with more options, allowing them to recharge according to their requirements and financial capacity. Overall, it will improve choices for consumers preferring not to use STVs bundled with data.

The amendment has been placed on TRAI's website (www.trai.gov.in). For any clarification/information, Shri. Vijay Kumar, Advisor (F&EA) may be contacted at Tel No. 011-20907773 or at email ID: fea1-div@trai.gov.in.

item.title: CCL’s Transformation Since 2014: From Higher Coal Production to Modern Mining, Sustainable Evacuation and Inclusive Development
item.dc:creator: Ministry of Coal
item.description: Ministry of Coal CCL’s Transformation Since 2014: From Higher Coal Production to Modern Mining, Sustainable Evacuation and Inclusive Development Central Coalfields Limited’s journey reflects a decade of expansion in production capacity, mechanisation, rail connectivity, technology adoption, renewable energy, financial strength and community development Posted On: 22 SEP 2026 12:52PM by PIB Delhi The Indian coal sector has undergone a significant transformation since 2014, driven by policy reforms, improved project clearances, infrastructure development, technology…
item.content:encoded:
Ministry of Coal
CCL’s Transformation Since 2014: From Higher Coal Production to Modern Mining, Sustainable Evacuation and Inclusive Development
Central Coalfields Limited’s journey reflects a decade of expansion in production capacity, mechanisation, rail connectivity, technology adoption, renewable energy, financial strength and community development
Posted On: 22 SEP 2026 12:52PM by PIB Delhi

The Indian coal sector has undergone a significant transformation since 2014, driven by policy reforms, improved project clearances, infrastructure development, technology adoption, greater mechanisation and a sharper focus on efficiency and energy security. Central Coalfields Limited (CCL), a subsidiary of Coal India Limited operating in the coalfields of Jharkhand, has emerged as an important example of this transformation.

The scale of CCL’s operational transformation is reflected most clearly in its coal production. From 50.0 Million Tonnes (MT) in FY 2013-14, CCL increased its production to 87.5 MT in FY 2024-25, the highest-ever production in the history of the company. Thus, over the period since 2013-14, CCL increased its production by nearly 75%. A major feature of CCL’s transformation has been the creation of additional mining capacity through new and expansion projects. Mega mines such as Amrapali (35 MTY), Magadh (51 MTY), Chandragupta OCP (15 MTY) and Kotre Basantpur Pachmo (5 MTY) have been developed during this period. Capacities of existing mines such as Karo, Konar and North Urimari etc. have also been expanded. Several more new mines and expansion projects are in the pipeline and are expected to further augment CCL’s production capacity in the coming years.

The transportation of incremental coal to its consumers through sustainable and efficient modes has been another major challenge. The transformation of CCL is therefore equally visible in the area of coal evacuation and logistics. Recognising that higher production must be supported by efficient evacuation infrastructure, the company has progressively invested in railway connectivity, Coal Handling Plants (CHPs), silos, rapid loading systems and First Mile Connectivity (FMC) projects.

The Tori-Shivpur rail corridor, one of the most critical railway links for the North Karanpura coalfields, has been progressively strengthened. The three-line railway corridor has the capacity to transport around 100 MT of coal per annum. To make coal transportation more sustainable and efficient, CCL is establishing CHPs and FMC projects. The 7.5 MTY North Urimari CHP has already been commissioned. Major CHP projects under development include Konar (5 MTY), KDH-Purnadih (7.5 MTY), Amrapali (25 MTY), Karo (7 MTY) and Magadh (51 MTY). These systems are designed to reduce dependence on road transportation, improve loading efficiency and facilitate direct rail evacuation.

Coking coal is critical for India’s steel sector, which continues to depend significantly on import. Recognising the strategic importance of import substitution, CCL has given a major thrust to increasing the availability of quality domestic washed coking coal, thereby contributing to foreign-exchange savings. The company is developing five new coking coal washeries with an aggregate capacity of 14.50 million tonnes per year (MTY). Significant progress has been made in advancing these projects.

CCL is also embracing emerging technologies to transform the way its operations are monitored and managed. In line with the growing adoption of Artificial Intelligence (AI), the company has established an AI-enabled Integrated Command and Control Centre (ICCC) to strengthen security, surveillance and operational oversight across its command areas. The centre integrates modern technologies to facilitate real-time monitoring and more effective decision-making.

Another important dimension of CCL’s transformation is its increasing emphasis on renewable energy and energy conservation. CCL currently has over 32 MW of installed solar capacity, including three ground-mounted projects with a combined capacity of 29 MW. A mega 100 MW solar power project is coming up in Giridih district along with a Battery Energy Storage System (BESS). These initiatives will increase the share of renewable energy in the company’s energy mix, reduce emissions and support its broader Net Zero commitment.

CCL is also making mining more sustainable through the adoption of modern and environment-friendly technologies. The company has adopted blast-free technologies such as surface miners and continuous miners, along with scientific restoration of overburden dumps, rainwater harvesting, plantation and mine reclamation measures. From zero production through surface miners and continuous miners before 2014, their share has now increased to nearly 70%. CCL is also utilising surplus mine water for the benefit of local communities, thereby converting a mining-related resource into an important instrument of community development.

CCL’s transformation has also been accompanied by a substantial strengthening of its financial position. Profit After Tax (PAT) increased from ₹808 crore in FY 2017-18 to ₹4,035 crore in FY 2024-25, while net worth increased from ₹3,816 crore to ₹16,464 crore during the same period.

The social dimension of CCL’s transformation is perhaps most visible through its CSR initiatives. CSR expenditure has evolved from programmes largely focused on basic infrastructure, drinking water, healthcare and education to larger, long-term interventions aimed at creating sustainable social assets and opportunities. In FY 2025-26, CCL reported total CSR expenditure of approximately ₹86 crore, against a CSR target of about ₹74 crore.

Among CCL’s most distinctive CSR initiatives is CCL Ke Lal & CCL Ki Laadli. The flagship programme provides talented students from underprivileged backgrounds with free residential schooling and engineering entrance coaching, with 40 students—20 boys and 20 girls—selected every year. The programme has enabled students from rural and mining-affected communities to pursue higher education at premier institutions such as IITs, NITs and other leading engineering institutions.

Similarly, the Sports Academy at Khelgaon, Ranchi, established through a partnership between CCL and the Government of Jharkhand, has emerged as another flagship intervention. Established using the infrastructure created for the 34th National Games, the academy is operated through the Jharkhand State Sports Promotion Society. Over the years, it has provided structured opportunities in sports, along with education and life-skills support, to young athletes. Athletes from the academy are bringing national as well as international medals. This initiative as won National CSR award twice.

Today, CCL is therefore much more than a coal-producing organisation. Its transformation since 2014 represents a transition towards higher production, greater productivity, expanded mining capacity, mechanised coal evacuation, stronger rail connectivity, renewable-energy adoption, improved environmental management, financial strengthening and a broader social-development role.

CCL’s journey demonstrates that the transformation of a coal company cannot be measured merely in million tonnes of production. The increase from around 50 MT to 87.5 MT is only one part of the story. The larger transformation lies in creating new mining capacity, building modern evacuation infrastructure, integrating CHPs and rail systems, adopting renewable energy, improving productivity and environmental management, and investing in communities through initiatives such as CCL Ke Lal & CCL Ki Laadli and the Khelgaon Sports Academy.

As India continues to pursue energy security alongside economic growth and environmental responsibility, CCL’s experience since 2014 illustrates how a traditional mining enterprise can progressively transform itself into a modern, technology-enabled, infrastructure-oriented and socially responsive organisation, while continuing to play a vital role in meeting the country’s energy requirements.

****

Prajith Kumar

(Release ID: 2313343)

item.title: SEMICON India 2026: From Silicon to Systems, India’s Semiconductor Journey on Display
item.dc:creator: Ministry of Electronics & IT

item.content:encoded:
Ministry of Electronics & IT
SEMICON India 2026: From Silicon to Systems, India’s Semiconductor Journey on Display
Exhibition Brought Together Industry, Academia, Start-ups and Policymakers, Showcasing India’s Expanding Capabilities Across the Semiconductor Value Chain
Posted On: 22 SEP 2026 12:10PM by PIB Delhi

For three days, Yashobhoomi in New Delhi served as a showcase of India’s growing semiconductor capabilities. From chip design and advanced packaging to materials, equipment, artificial intelligence and high-performance computing, SEMICON India 2026 brought together different parts of the semiconductor ecosystem under one roof.

Held from 17 to 19 September 2026, the fifth edition of SEMICON India was organised around the theme “Silicon to Systems: Building the Ecosystem”. The event brought together the global semiconductor ecosystem, including industry leaders, policymakers, investors, academia and start-ups. The 2026 edition featured more than 600 exhibiting companies from various countries, along with a Start-up Pavilion, Workforce Development Pavilion, country and state pavilions, and a hackathon.

The exhibition provided a glimpse into how India’s semiconductor journey is expanding beyond chip design towards a broader ecosystem covering manufacturing, packaging, research, materials, talent and system-level applications.

From Chip Design to Advanced Computing

One of the key features of the exhibition was the range of indigenous semiconductor and computing capabilities on display.

C-DAC showcased its work in high-performance computing and AI, including the AUM HPC-AI Processor and the RUDRA-AUM compute node. These efforts reflect the growing focus on developing indigenous capabilities not only at the chip level but also across computing systems.

The exhibition also highlighted the broader movement towards indigenous processor design. India’s semiconductor ecosystem has increasingly seen domestic start-ups and institutions develop processor technologies, application-specific chips and system solutions for sectors ranging from telecommunications and automotive applications to artificial intelligence and surveillance.

Chips for Everyday Applications

The exhibition also offered visitors a look at how semiconductor technologies can move from laboratories and design centres into everyday products.

Indian semiconductor companies and start-ups showcased solutions for applications such as smart appliances, connectivity, surveillance, industrial systems, energy management and automotive technologies.

Among the companies highlighted in the Indian chip-design ecosystem is Vervesemi Microelectronics, which is developing semiconductor solutions for motor control, energy meters and data acquisition applications. Its work includes chips for applications such as consumer appliances, electric mobility and drones.

Such application-specific semiconductor products demonstrate the importance of indigenous chip design in building a wider electronics manufacturing ecosystem.

RISC-V: Building Indigenous Processor Capabilities

C-DAC’s indigenous 64-bit RISC-V processor strengthens India’s capabilities in homegrown processor design and semiconductor technologies. Based on the open RISC-V architecture, it supports high-performance computing and emerging digital applications. Its adoption in indigenous solutions demonstrates India’s growing expertise in developing advanced processor technologies for next-generation computing, connectivity and digital infrastructure.

InCore Semiconductors showcased its work around indigenous RISC-V processor IPs and SoC design automation tools.

Its portfolio includes processor platforms designed for different levels of computing requirements, with applications spanning embedded systems and edge-AI use cases. InCore's processor IP has been silicon-proven across multiple customer chips and across technology nodes ranging from 180 nm to 16 nm.

The development of such processor technologies is an important component of the broader semiconductor design ecosystem, enabling Indian companies to develop products around domestically developed intellectual property.

Aheesa Technology has developed an indigenous internet connectivity device capable of delivering speeds of up to 1 Gbps, enabling Internet Service Providers (ISPs) to connect approximately 64 homes through a single Optical Line Terminal (OLT). The device runs on Vihan, a software platform developed entirely in India, and is powered by C-DAC’s 64-bit RISC-V processor. The solution represents a significant step towards strengthening India’s indigenous technology capabilities and advancing high-speed broadband connectivity through a fully Indian technology stack.

AI, Vision and Smart Surveillance

The growing convergence of semiconductors and artificial intelligence was another prominent feature of the exhibition.

Netrasemi, an Indian semiconductor start-up, showcased its work in AI-capable System-on-Chips (SoCs) for applications including secure surveillance, smart sensors, robotics, drones and mobility.

The company has taped out an indigenously designed AI SoC for CCTV Surveillance in the 12 nm process node, integrating AI/ML accelerators, vision processing and video engines. Its technologies are aimed at applications requiring intelligent vision and edge processing.

The exhibition demonstrated how advances in semiconductor design are increasingly enabling applications in areas such as machine vision, smart infrastructure, autonomous systems and surveillance.

Semiconductor Innovation Across the Value Chain

The exhibition was not limited to chips alone. It reflected the larger ecosystem required to develop and manufacture semiconductor products.

From materials and equipment to testing, packaging and system integration, the displays highlighted the interconnected nature of the semiconductor value chain.

This broader approach is central to Semicon 2.0, approved by the Union Cabinet in July 2026 with an outlay of ₹1,27,500 crore. The programme builds on the foundation laid by Semicon 1.0 and focuses on six strategic pillars -  design; machines and materials; more fabs; advanced packaging; research and development; and talent development.

From Start-ups to Research Institutions

The Start-up Pavilion provided another window into India's emerging semiconductor design ecosystem.

The Government's Design Linked Incentive (DLI) Scheme has supported domestic chip-design projects across areas including video surveillance, drone detection, energy meters, microprocessors, satellite communications, broadband and IoT SoCs.

The Chips to Startup (C2S) Programme is also supporting the development of semiconductor design capabilities among students, researchers, institutions and start-ups. The programme is aimed at creating a larger pool of skilled chip designers and strengthening the country's electronic system design capabilities.

More than one lakh engineers from over 500 organisations across the country, including 400 academic institutions and 100 start-ups, have been onboarded by the ChipIN Centre under the C2S Programme and DLI Scheme. They have been provided access to advanced chip-design tools, chip-design and fabrication services, and specialised training. Together, these institutions and start-ups have developed more than 300 chip designs for fabrication at foundries in India and abroad and have recorded over four crore hours of chip-design tool usage. This unprecedented scale has helped create the largest centralised chip-design user base at the ChipIN Centre.

From Policy to Production

The exhibition was held at a time when India's semiconductor ecosystem was moving from foundational policy support towards manufacturing and commercial production.

Under the Semicon India Programme, 12 semiconductor projects have been approved across six states, with investment commitments exceeding ₹1.64 lakh crore. Three facilities have already commenced commercial production.

At SEMICON India 2026, the emphasis was therefore not only on what India aims to build, but also on capabilities that are already being developed across design, manufacturing, packaging and related technologies.

Building the Complete Ecosystem

The theme “Silicon to Systems: Building the Ecosystem” captures the changing scope of India's semiconductor ambitions.

The semiconductor ecosystem requires much more than the fabrication of individual chips. It brings together chip designers, fabs, packaging and testing facilities, equipment and materials suppliers, research institutions, start-ups, system companies and a skilled workforce.

SEMICON India 2026 brought these different elements together, offering a view of an ecosystem developing across the value chain and connecting indigenous innovation with global semiconductor opportunities.

From processor design and RISC-V technologies to AI-enabled SoCs, motor-control chips, advanced computing and semiconductor manufacturing, the exhibition showcased the many layers of India's semiconductor journey.

The story on display at Yashobhoomi was therefore not just about the chip. It was about everything that surrounds it: the silicon, systems, people, research, manufacturing capabilities and partnerships needed to build a complete semiconductor ecosystem.

*****

Vinod Kumar / Vineeth Narayan / Vanshita Jaiswal / Kanishk Sharma

(Release ID: 2313324)

item.title: Corporate Social Responsibility in Coal India Limited: A Journey from Community Welfare to Inclusive Growth
item.dc:creator: Ministry of Coal
item.description: Ministry of Coal Corporate Social Responsibility in Coal India Limited: A Journey from Community Welfare to Inclusive Growth Coal India Limited’s CSR Expenditure Rises to Nearly Rs. 1,000 Crore Annually CIL Spends Rs. 7,276 Crore on CSR Against Statutory Requirement of Rs. 5,795 Crore During FY 2014-15 to FY 2025-26 Posted On: 22 SEP 2026 12:07PM by PIB Delhi For a company whose operations touch some of the most resource-poor and tribal-dominated districts of India, the idea of giving back to the community is not new to Coal India Limited (CIL). Long before the…
item.content:encoded:
Ministry of Coal
Corporate Social Responsibility in Coal India Limited: A Journey from Community Welfare to Inclusive Growth
Coal India Limited’s CSR Expenditure Rises to Nearly Rs. 1,000 Crore Annually
CIL Spends Rs. 7,276 Crore on CSR Against Statutory Requirement of Rs. 5,795 Crore During FY 2014-15 to FY 2025-26
Posted On: 22 SEP 2026 12:07PM by PIB Delhi

For a company whose operations touch some of the most resource-poor and tribal-dominated districts of India, the idea of giving back to the community is not new to Coal India Limited (CIL). Long before the Companies Act, 2013 made Corporate Social Responsibility a legal obligation for corporate India, CIL and its subsidiaries were already engaged in welfare activities in and around their mining areas under the Community Development (CD) Policy, 2005.

Under this earlier CD regime, subsidiaries supported villages within an 8 km radius of mining operations through drinking water facilities, health camps, and small infrastructure works — meaningful interventions that fostered harmony with peripheral communities. In the three years leading up to the Act (FY 2011-12 to 2013-14), CIL's consolidated CD spend varied from Rs. 82 cr. (FY 2011-12) to Rs. 409 cr. (FY 2013-14). The work being done was genuine and appreciated on the ground; what it lacked was a consistent, institutionalised framework to sustain and scale it year on year.

The Companies Act, 2013 and Section 135 changed this fundamentally. Companies were now required to spend a statutorily defined share of their average net profits on CSR, guided by Schedule VII themes and monitored by a Board-level CSR Committee. CIL built on this with its own policy architecture: at least 80% of annual CSR expenditure within a 25 km radius of mines and establishments, prioritising Project Affected Areas, with the balance for state and national initiatives. As a natural consequence of this local-area focus, more than 90% of CIL's CSR expenditure continues to be incurred within coal-bearing states — keeping the benefit anchored where the impact of mining is felt most directly.

The results are visible in the numbers. CIL has not merely met its statutory obligation — it has exceeded it consistently, year after year. Cumulatively, from FY 2014-15 to FY 2025-26, CIL has spent Rs. 7,276 crore against a statutory requirement of Rs. 5,795 crore. What is more striking is the trajectory within this: annual expenditure, once closer to Rs. 500 cr., the yearly outlay now touches almost Rs. 1,000 crore — placing CIL among the largest corporate CSR spenders in the country.

This growth in scale has been matched by a growth in purpose, with CIL's CSR converging deliberately with national missions. It was the number one CPSE contributor to the Swachh Vidyalaya Abhiyan, completing over 50,000 toilets in government schools; it was among the earliest major contributors to the PM-CARES Fund and ran an extensive COVID-19 relief programme, from dedicated hospitals in Odisha and Chhattisgarh to oxygen plants under “Mission Praana Vayu.” Flagship interventions have given the programme a distinct identity of its own — the NIRMAN scheme rewarding more than 1,300 UPSC aspirants from mining districts, the Thalassemia Bal Sewa Yojana enabling more than 1,000 life-saving bone marrow transplants, Nanha Sa Dil screening over 2 lakh children and curing over 1,700 of congenital heart disease, and the Scholarship Schemes with the Hon'ble Supreme Court of India reaching over 2,500 children. This has been matched by major healthcare and education infrastructure such as a 500-bed medical college and hospital at Angul and a cardiac care centre at Jharsuguda, together worth Rs. 596 crore, now serve as tertiary-care hubs for their respective regions, while Digital Vidya has commissioned over 2,300 smart classrooms and 500 ICT/STEM labs in government schools, alongside a 5,000-seater state library under construction in Ranchi.

The reach extends well beyond health and education. Skilling and livelihood programmes — including Project PRAGATI, tribal women's poultry support, and plastic engineering and multi-skill training — have benefited more than 48,000 people over the last four financial years alone. The Khelgaon Sports Academy, run in partnership with the Government of Jharkhand, has produced over 1,800 medals, including 15 at the international level; and landmark public-interest works — from the centenary building at IIT (ISM) Dhanbad to the illumination of Kolkata's Howrah Bridge — have carried CIL's CSR footprint into premier institutions and national landmarks alike.

Taken together, these efforts have touched an estimated 3.56 crore lives, directly and indirectly — with vulnerable groups including SC/ST communities, persons with disabilities, and women forming a significant share of the beneficiaries. This work has also meaningfully advanced India's own SDG commitments — health (SDG-3), education (SDG-4), gender equality (SDG-5), clean water and sanitation (SDG-6), and poverty alleviation (SDG-1).

None of this has happened by accident. CIL's CSR is governed by a structured output-outcome methodology — Annual Action Plans shaped by community needs, MoUs with defined deliverables and timelines, phase-wise fund release tied to milestones and Utilisation Certificates, and Impact Assessment Guidelines that make third-party evaluation mandatory for larger projects, layered atop internal, statutory, and CAG audit oversight. This architecture is now being strengthened at a sectoral level: on 8th September, the Ministry of Coal became the first Ministry of the Government of India to launch a sector-wide CSR framework, aimed at bringing greater consistency, convergence, and accountability to CSR efforts across the coal PSUs.

***

Prajith Kumar

(Release ID: 2313321)

item.content:encoded:
PIB Backgrounder
11th AYURVEDA DAY
Ayurveda for a Healthier Tomorrow
स्वस्थ भविष्य के लिए आयुर्वेद
Posted On: 22 SEP 2026 11:15AM by PIB Delhi

On the 11th Ayurveda Day, India celebrates a decade of bringing its 5,000-year-old healing system into every day, modern healthcare through evidence-led scientific research. Today, government clinics and hospitals across the country offer Ayurvedic treatments right alongside regular medical care. Free online doctor visits, insurance coverage, and top-tier scientific research are making these ancient wellness practices safer and far easier for everyone to access. Through strong global partnerships, India is showing the world how traditional wisdom and modern science can work together for a healthier future.

Ayurveda: The Foundations of Holistic Living

Ayurveda is a science of life that is over 5,000 years old. It has roots tracing back to the Rigveda. The word Ayurveda is derived from Ayu (life) and Veda (science), with its foundational goal -"Swasthasya Swasthya rakshnam, aturasya vikara prashaman"-being to maintain wellness in the healthy and cure illness in the sick.

Ayurveda defines true health as a harmonious balance of metabolic entities. This requires optimal alignment among the bio-energies (doshas), metabolic fire (agni), bodily tissues (dhatus), and waste elimination (malas), alongside a serene soul (atma), mind (manas), and senses (indriyas). By utilising the medicinal and therapeutic properties of plants, animal products, and minerals, which are also described in the Charaka Samhita and Sushruta Samhita, Ayurveda remains an ancient science with modern relevance. Central to this science is the principle that good health is a state of total alignment between the individual body, mind, and spirit - and the surrounding world.

To honour and promote this heritage, the Government marks September 23rd annually as Ayurveda Day, aligning with the autumnal equinox to reflect natural balance. Under the theme "Ayurveda for a Healthier Tomorrow," the Government is executing a national strategy to revive traditional healthcare.

The Government is also establishing an ecosystem to support the growth of the Ayurveda sector. This is through upgrading education, advancing evidence-based R&D, establishing drug standards, global outreach, and integrating Ayurveda with modern medicine. This whole-of-government approach runs in tandem with the growing global popularity of Ayurveda and allied traditional medical systems, including Yoga & Naturopathy, Unani, Siddha, and Homoeopathy.

Building the Health Infrastructure

The Government, through its National Ayush Mission (NAM), and the National Health Mission, is expanding, modernising and integrating Ayush systems, including Ayurveda, into mainstream public medicine. The two national missions run by the Ministry of Ayush and the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, respectively, are establishing Ayush clinics, hospitals, departments and community public health centres across the country.

The NAM is driving the expansion and integration of Ayush healthcare in the country. Between the financial years 2014–15 and 2025–26, the Central Government released over Rs.6,406.99 crore through the NAM to States and Union Territories to weave Ayush healthcare into conventional medical systems. The NHM is also supporting some of these initiatives. These initiatives include:

  • Modernising and Establishing Local Ayush clinics/health centres: Existing health clinics (dispensaries) are being modernised and upgraded into better-equipped wellness centres called Ayushman Arogya Mandirs (Ayush). This is a collaborative effort by the NHM, which supports Ayush AAMs by funding and training Ayush health personnel, and the NAM, which provides for the infrastructure, equipment/furniture, and medicines.
    • There are 12,260 Ayush AAMs functional (as on September 19, 2026). The NAM is targeting the setup of 12,500.
    • These Ayush AAMs are also being co-located with other community health centres through the NHM. The NHM helps offer Ayush services alongside standard medical care in 13,249 public health facilities nationwide.
      • Facilities Covered (as on December 30, 2025):
        • 6,302 Primary Health Centres
        • 3,191 Community Health Centres
        • 475 District Hospitals
        • 3,281 Other local health facilities
        • Staffing Support: The government funds salaries for 25,322 Ayush doctors and 5,666 Ayush paramedics working across various states and union territories.
    • A trained Ayurveda practitioner (a Bachelor of Ayurveda, Medicine and Surgery graduate) can be a Community Health Officer (CHO) to manage a village-level primary healthcare centre, providing a holistic approach to healthcare.
  • Combining Services Under One Roof: Adding traditional medicine counters and doctors inside standard public healthcare facilities, including local health centres and district hospitals.
  • Upgrading Existing Hospitals & Clinics: Repairing and updating standalone traditional medicine hospitals and clinics.
  • Building Better Facilities: Fixing run-down clinic buildings, moving clinics out of rented spaces into permanent ones, and constructing brand-new clinics in areas that currently have no traditional medicine services.
  • Building New Integrated Hospitals: Setting up new 10, 30, or 50-bed hospitals that combine different traditional medicine practices under one roof.
  • Providing Essential Medicines: Ensuring a steady, free supply of necessary traditional medicines to government clinics, hospitals, and teaching facilities.
  • Community Health Programs: Running public health drives tailored around traditional wellness and preventive care.
  • Awareness Campaigns: Creating educational programs, advertisements, and community outreach to teach people about health, wellness, and available treatments.
  • Opening New Medical Colleges: Building new traditional medicine colleges in states and regions that do not have enough public options for students.
  • Improving Medical Schools: Upgrading campus facilities, classrooms, and equipment for existing colleges, while adding advanced degrees, pharmacy programs, and paramedic training.

The Government is also expanding Ayush care by establishing Departments of Integrative Medicine at these central government hospitals:

  • Vardhman Mahavir Medical College (VMMC) & Safdarjung Hospital, and
  • Lady Hardinge Medical College.

These departments provide preventive, promotive, and therapeutic medical services, including a fully functional Panchakarma unit. Additionally, extended OPD services by Ayush Research Councils are available at:

  • Vardhman Mahavir Medical College (VMMC) & Safdarjung Hospital,
  • Lady Hardinge Medical College, and
  • Dr. Ram Manohar Lohia Hospital.

Ayush services are also available at the new All India Institute of Medical Sciences.

Telemedicine

The government offers a free telemedicine service–eSanjeevani–which has served over 50 crore patients. In addition to conventional medicine, eSanjeevani also offers Ayush OPD services, allowing patients to virtually consult doctors specialised in Ayurveda (and other Ayush services) directly through the platform.

Health Insurance

The government has updated insurance policies to cover Ayush treatments under health insurance plans. In 2024, the Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India (IRDAI) mandated that all insurers are required to offer products or add-ons covering all systems of medicine–including Ayurveda–under Board-approved underwriting policies.

On February 10, 2026, the All-India Institute of Ayurveda (AIIA), New Delhi, signed a Common Empanelment Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) with the General Insurance Council (GIC). This empanelled AIIA with all 32 general insurance companies in India, marking the first time an Ayush institution entered into a universal empanelment agreement for cashless treatment. The AIIA also launched a dedicated Ayush Health Insurance Helpline (1800-11-0008) to assist beneficiaries with their insurance-related queries and improve awareness about Ayush insurance coverage.

Inclusion of Ayurveda in the WHO ICD-11 Module

Ayurveda’s terms are now internationally recognised due to the World Health Organisation including it in the International Classification of Diseases 11th Revision Module. This inclusion will now enable clinicians worldwide to record ASU (Ayurveda, Siddha and Unani) diagnoses using standard codes, ensuring uniform interpretation across different regions and health facilities. It also makes it easier for insurance providers to process, approve, and reimburse Ayush treatments, help with research and development and policy-making, including making disease-control strategies for the future.

Development of Ayurveda Educational Infrastructure

An expanding Ayush health infrastructure also needs Ayush health personnel to run it. The NAM makes provisions for the expansion of education in Ayurveda through the establishment of undergraduate and postgraduate institutions, including pharmacy and para-medical programmes.

17 Ayush colleges have been approved for establishment across the country under the NAM, out of which 12 are centred on impacting Ayurvedic education. Ayurveda educational institutions–both public and private–are growing in number and helping build the sector. Across the country (as on March 13, 2026), there are:

  • 593 Ayurveda colleges,
  • 45,245 undergraduate Ayurveda seats, and
  • 5,673 post-graduate Ayurveda seats.

Beyond clinical training and academic expansion, establishing Ayurveda's credibility within contemporary medicine requires rigorous, evidence-based research and scientific validation.

Research and Development in Ayurveda

To advance research and development in Ayurveda, the government runs several schemes aimed at modernising traditional medical practices and strengthening drug development.

AYURGYAN Scheme

Central to these efforts is the AYURGYAN scheme, launched in 2021-22 by the Ministry of Ayush, which provides financial backing for R&D initiatives. Out of a total research funding pool of Rs. 17.79 crore across 34 projects, Ayurveda accounts for half of the portfolio, receiving Rs. 9.38 crore for 17 dedicated projects.

By early 2026, 11 specific research projects had been approved, with six focused on developing safety and efficacy dossiers for five key single Ayurvedic botanicals. These efforts reflect a growing academic output, contributing to 33 Ayurvedic-specific research publications between 2014-15 and 2025-26, and 77 total publications since 2001-02.

AYUR SWASTHYA Yojana

Complementing AYURGYAN scheme is the AYUR SWASTHYA Yojana (2021-2026), which provided financial assistance to government or non-profit Ayush organisations for research and development into Ayush clinical and drug research, education, public health initiatives, and for the upgradation of facilities to Centres of Excellence.

Out of 25 projects supported through late 2025, 22 focused on or incorporated Ayurveda interventions. The scheme established 28 specialised Centres of Excellence, with 22 dedicated to advancing Ayurveda-centric research and healthcare delivery.

Central Council for Research in Ayurvedic Sciences (CCRAS)

At the institutional level, the Central Council for Research in Ayurvedic Sciences (CCRAS)-one of five autonomous research bodies under the Ministry-leads the scientific formulation, coordination, and promotion of Ayurvedic studies nationwide. Operating through a network of 30 national and regional institutes, CCRAS builds research capacity through fellowships, training programs, and targeted student initiatives such as the SPARK Programme.

SPARK Programme

The Studentship Programme for Ayurveda Research Ken (SPARK) fosters research interest and aptitude among undergraduate Ayurveda students. The programme supports short-term independent projects to encourage students to conduct research in Ayurveda. Between 2022-23 and 2024-25, 289 Ayurveda colleges benefited through the SPARK programme.

AI-Translation of Ayurveda Research

To make scientific knowledge accessible to everyone, the CCRAS partnered with Anuvadini AI-an artificial intelligence translation platform developed by the Ministry of Education’s AICTE-in March 2026. Through this collaboration, CCRAS is translating its extensive research findings, educational resources, and quarterly medical journals into 13 regional Indian languages.

By breaking down language barriers, this initiative democratises access to Ayurvedic medical research, ensuring that students, practitioners, and the general public across India can easily read and learn from these scientific developments.

Development of Medicinal Plants

The Government actively supports farmers and research bodies in conserving, cultivating, and processing therapeutic herbs. It does so by bridging supply chain gaps, incentivising farmers while empowering local communities and maintaining pharmaceutical standards.

Strengthening Regulatory Standards: Drug Safety and Consumer Foods

As the Ayurveda market booms, the Government is also establishing a legal framework to ensure that the products are safe for consumers.

Quality Control of Medicines

Ayurvedic medicines are strictly regulated under the Drugs & Cosmetics Act, 1940, and the Drugs Rules, 1945. Under these legal frameworks:

  • Manufacturers must adhere to Good Manufacturing Practices (GMP), prove drug safety and efficacy, and meet pharmacopoeia standards.
  • Government Drug Inspectors conduct routine sampling and testing to maintain quality control, supported by a specialised Ayush vertical established within the Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation (CDSCO).

To streamline compliance, the government launched the e-Aushadhi portal for paperless processing and real-time tracking of drug manufacturing license applications.

Ayurveda Aahara

Extending these safety principles from pharmaceuticals to nutrition, the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI), in collaboration with the Ministry of Ayush, introduced a standardised regulation for Ayurveda Aahara. This initiative establishes a product list of authentic Ayurvedic dietary items based on authoritative classical texts. This list is also crucial for licensing and registration of traditional food manufacturers. It creates a transparent, regulated sector for traditional food manufacturers while boosting consumer confidence in India and globally.

Expanding International Partnerships and Diplomatic Ties

For the global acceptance and market integration of Ayush, the Government has established strategic bilateral partnerships, research collaborations, and educational exchanges worldwide. This is through the signing of various country-to-country agreements, research collaborations, educational exchange programmes, and global certification of medicines.

International Collaborations

Through strategic international partnerships, collaborative research frameworks, academic chair appointments, and specialised scholarship programs, the country continues to establish a strong international footprint in holistic healthcare and integrative medicine. India has signed various MoUs, such as:

  • 27 Country-to-Country MoUs for cooperation in traditional medicine and Homoeopathy.
  • 16 MoUs with international institutes for setting up Ayush Academic Chairs.
  • 57 Institute-to-Institute MoUs for collaborative research and academics.
  • 3 Country-to-Country MoUs signed in 2025-26 in Angola, Kazakhstan and Tanzania and 6 institute-level MoUs signed with institutions in Ghana, South Africa, Réunion Island, Germany, Malaysia and Mongolia, and an academic chair MoU with Oman.

This global footprint is further supported by:

  • 46 Ayush Information Cells established across 43 foreign nations.
  • 104 scholarships offered to foreign nationals under the International Ayush Fellowship/Scholarship Program.

Leading Global Summits, Frameworks, and Strategic Agreements

India is now a global hub for policy and standards in traditional medicine. In December 2025, New Delhi hosted the Second WHO Global Summit on Traditional Medicine at Bharat Mandapam. The event gathered delegates from over 100 countries and 22 health ministers under the theme "Restoring Balance: The Science and Practice of Health and Well-being". Attendees adopted the Delhi Declaration, encouraging member states to bring traditional medicine into primary healthcare through proven scientific methods.

Setting International Standards and Promoting Cultural Diplomacy

Setting strict quality and training standards drives India's global strategy. The WHO Global Traditional Medicine Centre in Jamnagar, Gujarat, acts as a primary research and policy hub. The Ministry of Ayush partnered with the WHO to create standard training guides for Ayurveda and Unani. It also co-hosted an herbal drug regulation workshop with 17 nations and presented research at the International Conference on the Science of Botanicals in the US. Cultural outreach continues to expand.

The 11th International Day of Yoga in June 2025 featured roughly 2,000 events across 191 countries. Meanwhile, daily Yoga sessions at World Expo 2025 in Osaka, Japan, turned the Indian Pavilion into one of the event's most visited highlights.

Multilateral Cooperation and Medical Value Travel

India continues to embed traditional healthcare into major international alliances. Following recent BRICS statements, including the Rio de Janeiro Declaration, the 16th BRICS Health Ministers' Meeting in Chandigarh established a dedicated Expert Working Group on Traditional, Complementary, and Integrative Medicine.

At the same time, the government is making it easier for foreign patients to seek natural care in India. Specialised Ayush Visa options now streamline travel, offering the M-3 visa for patients and the M-4 visa for their accompanying caregivers. This initiative supports India’s aim to be a global medical tourism hub.

Union Budget 2026-27 Allocations for the Ayush Sector

The Union Budget’s (2026-27) allocation of Rs. 4,408 crores for the Ministry of Ayush highlights the government’s commitment to strengthening Ayush healthcare systems across the country, promoting evidence-based research and innovation, and strengthening other Ayush-related infrastructure and global outreach. The Budget announced several key initiatives:

  • Establishment of three new All India Institutes of Ayurveda (AIIA) to strengthen education, clinical services and research.
  • Upgradation of Ayush pharmacies and Drug Testing Laboratories to ensure quality, standardisation and availability of skilled manpower.
  • Upgradation of the WHO Global Traditional Medicine Centre, Jamnagar, to promote evidence-based research and global outreach in traditional medicine.

Integrating Tradition with Modern Health Systems

Ayurveda’s journey from an inherited knowledge tradition to an increasingly institutionalised component of contemporary healthcare reflects its evolving relevance in modern society. The expansion of healthcare infrastructure, education, research, regulatory mechanisms, digital access, and international collaborations has created a broader ecosystem for its development and responsible integration. The growing emphasis on scientific validation, quality standards, and evidence-based research is particularly significant in strengthening its contemporary relevance.

At the same time, Ayurveda's integration into public health systems and its expanding global partnerships show how traditional knowledge can engage with modern institutions and scientific inquiry. Ayurveda’s continuing evolution thus represents a dynamic interface between India’s civilisational knowledge, contemporary healthcare systems and the pursuit of holistic well-being.

item.content:encoded:
Prime Minister's Office
Prime Minister shares a Sanskrit Subhashitam, highlighting the journey towards happiness, prosperity, and well-being through righteousness
Posted On: 22 SEP 2026 9:38AM by PIB Delhi

Prime Minister Shri Narendra Modi shared a Sanskrit Subhashitam today, highlighting the journey towards happiness, prosperity, and well-being through righteousness and noble guidance.  

The Prime Minister wrote on X;

"सुत्रामाणं पृथिवीं द्यामनेहसं सुशर्माणमदितिं सुप्रणीतिम् ।

दैवीं नावं स्वरित्रामनागसो अस्रवन्तीमा रुहेमा स्वस्तये॥"  

May human beings seek refuge in the ever-protecting earth and the vast, boundless heavens, which provide secure shelter and uphold righteousness. Freed from sin and guided along the auspicious path, may we embark upon the divine boat, strong, well-crafted, and equipped with noble oars, and safely cross over to happiness, prosperity, and well-being.

item.content:encoded:
Office of Principal Scientific Advisor to GoI
Office of PSA convenes first ‘State Governments Nodal Officers Meeting’ to strengthen state-level coordination for wider access to Scientific and R&D infrastructure
I-STEM opens pathways for State Universities, institutions and R&D facilities to connect with the National Scientific Ecosystem
I-STEM expands State-level reach with 31,000+ scientific instruments and 4,000 institutions
Posted On: 21 SEP 2026 9:17PM by PIB Delhi

Dr. (Mrs.) Parvinder Maini, Scientific Secretary, Office of PSA to the Government of India chaired the first “State Governments Nodal Officers Meeting” for the I-STEM Portal on 21st September 2026. The meeting focused on strengthening the participation of State Governments in the I-STEM ecosystem and facilitating the onboarding and effective utilisation of publicly funded scientific infrastructure across States.

I-STEM was conceived and supported by the Office of the PSA and launched by the Hon’ble Prime Minister in January 2020. The platform has expanded into a national resource with more than 31,000 scientific instruments across nearly 4,000 institutions and over 65,000 registered users. By improving the utilisation of existing infrastructure, reducing duplication of investments and facilitating access to specialised facilities, I-STEM is strengthening the research and innovation ecosystem across the country. Also, the listing of publicly funded equipment costing above ₹20 lakh on I-STEM, further strengthens the framework for shared access and optimal utilisation of scientific infrastructure.

The meeting brought together State Government Nodal Officers from 23 States and 4 UTs, along with representatives from the Office of the PSA and I-STEM, to discuss mechanisms for integrating State-level universities, research institutions, laboratories and other R&D facilities with the national I-STEM platform. The meeting included an overview of I-STEM, a detailed orientation on the platform, and an interactive discussion with the Nodal Officers.

In her keynote address, Dr. (Mrs.) Parvinder Maini, Scientific Secretary, Office of PSA, highlighted the need to ensure that India’s investments in scientific and R&D infrastructure are discoverable, accessible and optimally utilised. She emphasised the role of Nodal Officers in facilitating institutional onboarding, equipment listing, wider access and effective utilisation of facilities, while addressing practical issues related to coordination and implementation. She also highlighted the importance of initiatives such as One Nation One Subscription (ONOS) in enabling wider access to high-quality scholarly resources and strengthening the research ecosystem. She further underscored that the larger objective should be to ensure that scientific infrastructure and knowledge resources created through public investment are accessible to the wider R&D and innovation ecosystem and deliver greater value to the country.

Dr. Vishal Choudhary, Scientist ‘F’, Office of PSA, provided an overview of the I-STEM Portal, while Dr. Harilal Bhaskar, COO/National Coordinator, I-STEM, conducted the detailed orientation on the platform and its functionalities. The orientation covered the process of onboarding institutions, listing scientific equipment and enabling wider access to publicly funded R&D infrastructure.

The meeting also highlighted the importance of I-STEM for State universities, colleges, technical institutions and emerging innovation ecosystems, particularly where access to specialised scientific infrastructure may be limited. It was also emphasized that all other existing similar portals (like ANALYTICS portal of CSIR) are being integrated with I-STEM through API linkages.

The deliberations and stakeholder interventions underscored the following key priorities:

  • Strengthening institutional onboarding: Encouraging universities, research institutions and R&D laboratories under State Governments to register on I-STEM as both users and facility providers.
  • Expanding access: Enabling researchers, startups, MSMEs and industry to discover and access specialised scientific infrastructure available across institutions and States.
  • Improving utilisation: Promoting wider and more efficient use of existing publicly funded scientific equipment and facilities.
  • Supporting infrastructure planning: Using the national infrastructure landscape available through I-STEM to inform future investments and minimise duplication.
  • Strengthening State-level coordination: Enabling State Government Nodal Officers to act as a link between State Governments, their institutions and the national I-STEM ecosystem, supporting onboarding, equipment listing, awareness and effective utilisation.

The meeting concluded with an emphasis on strengthening coordination between State-level R&D infrastructure and the national science, technology and innovation ecosystem. The State Government Nodal Officers were encouraged to facilitate wider adoption of I-STEM within their respective States and address practical issues relating to institutional onboarding, equipment listing, access, utilisation and coordination.

item.content:encoded:
Ministry of Science & Technology
CSIR-CRRI to lend scientific support and join hands with VMRDA and GVMC for better, safer roads in Visakhapatnam
Posted On: 21 SEP 2026 8:46PM by PIB Delhi

A high-level meeting convened by the Hon'ble Member of Parliament, Visakhapatnam, Shri M. Bharath Garu, was held today at the office of the Visakhapatnam Metropolitan Region Development Authority (VMRDA), Visakhapatnam, to chart a scientific road-improvement programme for the city. A senior delegation of the CSIR-Central Road Research Institute (CSIR-CRRI), New Delhi, led by its Director Dr. Ch. Ravi Sekhar, took part in the meeting along with senior officers of the city and the metropolitan region.

The meeting was attended, among others, by Shri Ketan Garg, IAS, Municipal Commissioner, Greater Visakhapatnam Municipal Corporation (GVMC); Shri P. V. V. Satyanarayana Raju, Chief Engineer, GVMC; and Shri Vinay Kumar, Chief Engineer, VMRDA. From CSIR-CRRI, Dr. G. Bharat, Dr. Sampath Kumar P., Dr. P. S. Prasad and Dr.K.Ravinder presented the Institute's technologies for flexible pavements, performance evaluation of roads, subgrade improvement for weak and waterlogged ground, and urban road safety.

The interaction comes at a significant moment for the city, with GVMC supported by VMRDA having taken up a major programme for the upgradation of gravel and WBM roads to BT/CC standards and the development of end-to-end pavements with allied infrastructure across eight constituencies, covering around 228 km of roads, 34 km of central medians, over 1,550 street lights and improvement of key junctions. CSIR-CRRI’s scientific expertise is expected to strengthen the planning, quality and long-term durability of such works.

Opening the deliberations, the Hon'ble MP outlined the city's priorities, including bridge assessments, quality control on road projects, deployment of an i-RASTE-type intelligent road-safety system and a end to end pavement solution for Visakhapatnam, and structured training for contractors and engineers on various road-related aspects. He observed that Visakhapatnam, with its major port, industrial base, growing metropolitan region and long, demanding coastline, needs durable, scientifically engineered roads.

 

The detailed discussion identified a wide set of areas in which CSIR-CRRI would study the problems and propose solutions. These include relaying of roads through end-to-end paving, new roads and reconditioning of existing ones; scientific study and remedies for erosion of roads, urban flooding and coastal erosion; “right-to-walk” pedestrian facilities; road and road-safety audits; rationalisation of speed breakers; and a modern Road Asset Management System for the city's road network.

To place this cooperation on a firm and lasting footing, Dr. Ch. Ravi Sekhar, Director CRRI and Dr. Vinod Karar, chief scientist assured speedy execution on the modalities of the proposed Memoranda of Agreement/Understanding (MoA/MoU): one between CSIR-CRRI and GVMC and another between CSIR-CRRI and VMRDA covering the above areas of work. These agreements will allow CSIR-CRRI's seventy-five years of road-research expertise to be applied directly and impartially to the city’s roads.

The Hon'ble MP, Shri M. Bharath Garu, stressed the need for detailed planning of the proposed solutions and a clear, time-bound action plan, so that Visakhapatnam can have the best roads in the country. He suggested to study holistically for the world class infrastructure in Visakhapatnam. He urged the civic bodies and CSIR-CRRI to translate the day’s deliberations into work on the ground at the earliest.

Dr. Ch. Ravi Sekhar, Director, CSIR-CRRI, assured the gathering that the Institute is fully committed to partnering with GVMC and VMRDA, and that it will promptly follow up with nomination of nodal officers, joint site visits and identification of priority stretches.

As a first step, the CSIR-CRRI team, along with Shri Shanti Raju, Executive engineer, GVMC carried out survey of selected stretches of Visakhapatnam's roads to assess the road conditions, geometric design, road safety aspects, road signs, junction improvements, pedestrian facilities, and road distress parameters.
